309.title: A song without words
309.hook: Hasidic prayer uses wordless melodies to lift the heart
309.howItsDone: Hasidic communities sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at gatherings called farbrengens or tisches, before prayer and at weddings; many other Jewish communities have adopted them too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebbe of Nemirov chopped wood in secret, and a skeptic said: if not higher. Did you do one hidden kindness? Today, a sound instead of a story. Day three hundred nine.

Think of a tune you hum when nobody's listening. In the car. Doing dishes. Rocking a baby at two in the morning. There are no words, or you've forgotten them, and it doesn't matter. The humming does something words can't. It settles you. Now picture a long table on a Friday night, a hundred people around it, and the rebbe at the head. Someone starts a slow melody. Yai, dai, dai. Nobody sings a single word. And the whole room starts to rise. Today's word: niggun.
screen: `A TUNE HUMMED IN THE CAR.` → `A HUNDRED PEOPLE AT A TABLE.` → `YAI, DAI, DAI.`

segments.voice: Niggun means melody. Hasidism made it into something close to a form of prayer. Many niggunim have no words at all, just sounds: yai-dai-dai, bim-bam, ai-ai-ai. Some are slow and aching, some are fast and joyful, built for dancing. Every Hasidic community has its own, passed down from rebbe to disciple, some for more than two hundred years. They're sung at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, before prayer, at weddings. Why no words? A saying often attributed to Shneur Zalman of Liadi puts it this way: words are the pen of the heart, but melody is the pen of the soul. Words can only say what you already understand. A melody can carry what you can't put into words: longing, grief, joy, a closeness to God that sentences would only shrink. There's a hint in the Bible, too. When the prophet Elisha needed to prophesy, he said: "But now bring me a minstrel." As the musician played, the hand of the Lord came on him. In Hebrew, the word for playing there comes from the same root as niggun. Music, in that story, opens a door. And a niggun has a shape: it often starts low and slow, repeats and repeats, climbs, and then returns. That repetition is the point. By the sixth or seventh time, you stop thinking about the tune. You're just inside it. That's the lift Hasidim are after. Not performance. Not a good voice. Just a heart carried upward on a sound.
screen: `NIGGUN: A MELODY.` · `YAI-DAI-DAI, NO WORDS.` · `THE PEN OF THE SOUL.` · `ELISHA: BRING ME A MINSTREL.` · then, large: `A SONG WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum a wordless tune. Settle, and breathe. Let a simple melody come, any melody, or make one up with three or four notes. Hum it quietly. If you're somewhere you can't make sound, hum it inside. Don't try to sing well. Just repeat it. Again. Again. Let it get a little slower each time. Notice when you stop thinking about the tune and just rest inside it. If you pray, you can let the melody be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Niggun. A Hasidic melody, often with no words, sung over and over until the heart lifts. Words are the pen of the heart; melody, the pen of the soul.
Your line: a song with no words. Today, when words run out, in a hard moment or a happy one, hum instead. Day three hundred nine.

310.title: Raising the sparks
310.hook: holy sparks hide in everything, and ordinary acts done with care can lift them
310.howItsDone: Hasidim speak of raising sparks through blessings, prayer and everyday acts done with intention, and many Jews today use tikkun olam for acts of justice and repair in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, niggun, the Hasidic melody with no words. Your line was a song with no words. Did you hum when words ran out? Day three hundred ten.

Most of your day isn't dramatic. You wash a cup. You answer an email. You fold a shirt, buy bread, sweep a floor. It can feel like the real life, the important, spiritual part, is happening somewhere else, and all this is just maintenance. Hasidism has a very old picture that turns that upside down. It says hidden inside the cup, the email, the shirt and the bread are sparks of holiness, waiting. And the way you handle them can set them free. Today's word: tikkun.
screen: `WASH A CUP. FOLD A SHIRT.` → `JUST MAINTENANCE?` → `SPARKS HIDDEN IN THE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repair, or mending, setting something right. The picture behind it comes from Rabbi Isaac Luria, a kabbalist in the town of Safed in the fifteen hundreds, whose teachings were written down mostly by his student, Chaim Vital. In Luria's picture, when God made the world, divine light was poured into vessels that couldn't hold it. The vessels shattered. Sparks of holy light scattered everywhere and fell into the world, trapped in shells, hidden in all things. The work of history is tikkun: gathering those sparks and lifting them back. That sounds cosmic, and it is. But the Baal Shem Tov and the Hasidim brought it down to the kitchen. They taught that sparks wait everywhere: in food, in work, in conversation, even in the people and places you happen to cross. When you eat with a blessing, work honestly, speak kindly, do an ordinary thing with care, you lift the spark inside it. Nothing is too small to matter. You may know a related phrase: tikkun olam, repairing the world. It's older than people think. The Mishnah uses it for rules made for the good order of society, and the Aleinu prayer speaks of perfecting the world under the kingdom of the Almighty. Today many Jews use it for justice and social action. The Hasidic version is quieter. The repair begins with how you wash this cup, right now.
screen: `TIKKUN: REPAIR.` · `LURIA: THE VESSELS SHATTERED.` · `SPARKS IN FOOD, WORK AND WORDS.` · `TIKKUN OLAM: REPAIR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `LIFT THE SPARKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one chore with care. Settle, and breathe. Choose a small task in front of you or coming up soon. Washing a dish. Making a bed. Tidying a desk. When you do it, do it slowly, and fully. Feel the water, the fabric, the weight of things. Imagine there's a spark inside it, waiting for someone to do this well. For now, just picture yourself doing it that way. If you pray, you can say a word of blessing before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Tikkun. Repair. In Luria's picture, holy sparks are scattered through everything, and ordinary acts done with care lift them back.
Your line: lift the sparks. Today, pick one boring task and do it as if something holy were hidden inside it. Day three hundred ten.

311.title: The Maggid's circle
311.hook: the Maggid of Mezeritch taught a circle of students who carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe
311.howItsDone: Many Hasidic communities trace their lineage back through their founding rebbe to the Maggid of Mezeritch and the Baal Shem Tov, and they retell the Maggid's teachings at gatherings and on the anniversary of his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun: holy sparks hidden in ordinary things. Your line was lift the sparks. Did one boring task get done with care? Day three hundred eleven.

Think of the best teacher you ever had. Chances are you can't remember a single lecture word for word. What you remember is how they were. How they listened. How they walked into a room. One Hasidic student put it perfectly. He said he didn't go to his teacher to hear him teach Torah. He went to watch how he laced and unlaced his boots. That teacher was the Maggid of Mezeritch, and the students who sat in his house would carry Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
screen: `THE BEST TEACHER YOU EVER HAD.` → `NOT THE LECTURE. THE WAY THEY WERE.` → `WATCHING HIM LACE HIS BOOTS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Dov Ber was called the Maggid, which means the preacher, the one who tells. He was a serious scholar who came to the Baal Shem Tov, the tradition says, as something of a skeptic, and left as his disciple. After the Baal Shem Tov died in 1760, it was the Maggid who, as the tradition tells it, became the center of the movement. He wasn't a traveler. He was often ill, and he taught from his home in the small town of Mezeritch, in what is now Ukraine. But the students who came to him were extraordinary. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, who would found Chabad. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, the defense attorney. Zusya of Anipoli, who worried about not being Zusya, and his brother Elimelech of Lizhensk. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, who later led a group of Hasidim to the Land of Israel. And many more. When the Maggid died in 1772, something unusual happened. There was no single heir. Instead, his students went home, to Belarus, Galicia, Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine, and each became a teacher in his own place. One circle in one house turned into dozens of Hasidic communities, many of which still exist, each with its own melodies and customs. The very first teaching of Pirkei Avot tells the sages to raise many disciples. The Maggid did exactly that. His teaching didn't stay in Mezeritch. It went out the door, in the boots of his students.
screen: `MAGGID: THE ONE WHO TELLS.` · `A SMALL HOUSE IN MEZERITCH.` · `SHNEUR ZALMAN, LEVI YITZCHAK, ZUSYA.` · `NO SINGLE HEIR: MANY TEACHERS.` · then, large: `PASS IT ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on one thing you learned. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this year. Of everything you've heard, a story, a word, a saying, a practice, which one has stayed with you? Let it come. Now think of one person who might need it. Not as a lecture. The way the Maggid's students carried him: by how they lived. How could you pass this on, in a sentence, or in the way you act today? If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever taught you. The bell holds the time.
The Maggid's circle. The students of Dov Ber of Mezeritch, who went home after his death and carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
Your line: pass it on. Today, share one thing you've learned with someone who might need it, in a word or in the way you live it. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: Opponents and neighbors
312.hook: Hasidism met fierce opposition from the Vilna Gaon's circle; today both ways of life thrive
312.howItsDone: Today Hasidic communities and the Lithuanian-style yeshiva world live side by side in places like Jerusalem, Bnei Brak and Brooklyn, each with its own customs, and study many of the same texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maggid's circle carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe. Your line was pass it on. Did you share one thing you've learned? Today, the people who pushed back. Day three hundred twelve.

Every family has its big argument. The one about how things should be done. How holidays work. What really matters. Voices get raised, doors get slammed, and for a while it seems like there's no way back. For the last two weeks we've been hearing Hasidic stories. But Hasidism didn't spread without a fight. Some of the greatest rabbis of the age thought it was a dangerous mistake, and said so, loudly. Today: the opponents, and what happened to the argument. Today's word: Mitnagdim.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY'S BIG ARGUMENT.` → `HASIDISM DIDN'T SPREAD QUIETLY.` → `THE OPPONENTS.`

segments.voice: Mitnagdim means opponents, the ones who stood against. Their great figure was Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, called the Vilna Gaon, the genius of Vilna, one of the most brilliant Torah scholars in centuries. He and his circle were alarmed by the new movement. The Hasidim changed the prayer book and prayed at their own times. They put enormous weight on the rebbe. Some were accused of neglecting deep Talmud study for joy and song. For people who had lived through false messiahs a century earlier, it looked risky. In 1772, the community of Vilna declared a ban against the Hasidim. The conflict was bitter. There were bans on both sides, harsh words, even denunciations to the government. It's not a pretty chapter, and nobody tells it as one. The tradition says Shneur Zalman once came to Vilna hoping to make peace, and the Gaon would not see him. But here's the rest of the story. The argument changed both sides. The Gaon's student, Chaim of Volozhin, founded a great yeshiva, and his teaching stressed Torah study as the heart of Jewish life. Hasidism, in turn, took learning seriously, too. By the eighteen hundreds, the two camps were facing new challenges together. Today, the Hasidic world and the yeshiva world, sometimes called Litvish, from Lithuania, both flourish, often on the same streets. The Talmud, describing the old schools of Hillel and Shammai, says: these and these are the words of the living God. Two paths. Both endure.
screen: `MITNAGDIM: THE OPPONENTS.` · `THE VILNA GAON.` · `1772: A BITTER BAN.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `BOTH PATHS ENDURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a rival school. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group whose way of doing things rubs you the wrong way. Another team, another school, another style of doing what you do. Not an enemy. A rival. Now ask one honest question: what do they protect that I might forget? What do they get right? You don't have to agree with them. Just find the one true thing in their way. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Mitnagdim. The opponents of early Hasidism, led by the Vilna Gaon. The argument was bitter; today both ways of life thrive side by side.
Your line: both paths endure. Today, when you hear yourself dismissing people who do things differently, name one thing they do well. Day three hundred twelve.

313.title: The story that healed
313.hook: a lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem danced while praying, and began to dance himself
313.howItsDone: Hasidim tell stories of their rebbes at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, and especially on a teacher's yahrzeit, the anniversary of his death, as a way of drawing close to his holiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mitnagdim, and a bitter argument both sides survived. Your line was both paths endure. Did you find one thing a rival does well? Today, the last of our Hasidic stories. Day three hundred thirteen.

You've probably had this happen. Someone starts telling a story about a person you both loved, a grandparent, an old friend, and as they tell it, they start doing the voice. The walk. The laugh. And for a moment, the person is almost in the room. A good story doesn't just describe something. It brings it back. Hasidim believed this deeply. For twenty days we've been hearing their stories. Today, the story they tell about why they tell stories at all.
screen: `DOING GRANDPA'S VOICE.` → `FOR A MOMENT, HE'S IN THE ROOM.` → `A STORY ABOUT STORIES.`

segments.voice: A rabbi, whose grandfather had been a student of the Baal Shem Tov, was once asked to tell a story. He said: a story ought to be told so that it helps. And he told this one. My grandfather was lame. One day people asked him to tell a story about his teacher, the Baal Shem Tov. So he told them how the holy Baal Shem used to leap and dance while he prayed. And as he told it, my grandfather stood up. He got so carried away by the story that he began to leap and dance, to show how his master had done it. And from that hour on, he was healed. That, said the rabbi, is how to tell a story. It's one small story, but it holds the whole movement inside it. Hasidim didn't treat their tales as entertainment. They told them at the Shabbat table, at the end of a festival, on the anniversary of a teacher's death, believing that telling of a holy deed could stir up the same holiness in the people listening. The story doesn't only remember. It happens again. Think about what we've heard in this stretch: the Baal Shem Tov and serving with joy, the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, the tailor, the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, the crying baby, the tavern, the rebbe with the axe, the niggun, the sparks, the Maggid's circle, the Mitnagdim. Each one, told well, still moves someone. Tomorrow, a new stretch: the Psalms, the songs of Jewish prayer.
screen: `A STORY SHOULD HELP.` · `THE BAAL SHEM DANCED AS HE PRAYED.` · `A LAME MAN STANDS UP.` · `THE STORY HAPPENS AGAIN.` · then, large: `TELL IT AND IT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell a story that lifts someone. Settle, and breathe. Look back over these Hasidic tales, or over your own life, and pick one story that lifts you. Maybe the shepherd boy's whistle. Maybe something your grandmother did. Tell it to yourself, quietly, in your own words, the way you'd tell it to a friend. Notice where it lifts. Now think of one person who might need to hear it this week. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people in your stories. The bell holds the time.
The story that healed. A lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem Tov danced in prayer, and began to dance himself. That's how to tell a story.
Your line: tell it and it happens. Today, tell someone a story that lifts, and tell it like you mean it. Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: The Psalms
314.hook: one hundred and fifty songs linked to David, woven through every Jewish prayer service
314.howItsDone: Psalms fill the Jewish prayer book, from the morning service to Friday night; many Jews also recite Tehillim privately, in times of trouble, for the sick, and at gravesides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of our Hasidic stories: the story that healed. Your line was tell it and it happens. Did you tell a story that lifts? Today, a new stretch begins. Day three hundred fourteen.

Walk into a hospital waiting room in Jerusalem and you may see someone rocking gently over a small book, lips moving. On a bus, a teenager doing the same. At a graveside, a whole family. At a wedding, a grandmother. It's very often the same book. Not the prayer book. Not the Torah scroll. A collection of one hundred and fifty ancient songs, the one part of the Bible that Jews carry with them almost everywhere. For the next two weeks, we open it. Today's word: Tehillim.
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `A BUS, A GRAVESIDE, A WEDDING.` → `THE SAME SMALL BOOK.`

segments.voice: Tehillim is the Hebrew name for the Book of Psalms. It means praises, from the same root as hallelujah. There are one hundred and fifty of them, and they're gathered into five smaller books. An old midrash notices the pattern: Moses gave Israel five books of Torah, and David gave Israel five books of Psalms. Jewish tradition links the Psalms to King David, the shepherd who played the harp. But the book itself is honest that it isn't only his. Some psalms are headed for Asaph, some for the sons of Korah, two for Solomon, and Psalm ninety is called a prayer of Moses. Many have no name at all. What's in them? Everything. Praise and thanks, yes. But also fear, anger, loneliness, guilt, homesickness, questions that sound almost like accusations. "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise shall continually be in my mouth." And elsewhere, in the same book: why do You hide Your face? That range is why people reach for them. Whatever you're feeling, there's a psalm that has already felt it. And Jewish prayer is full of them. The morning service opens with a stretch of psalms. Friday night welcomes Shabbat with psalms. Festivals have their own psalms of praise. Each day of the week has its own psalm. Over the next two weeks, we'll meet many of them: the tree by the stream, the shepherd, the clean hands, the rivers of Babylon. Songs of praise, and much more.
screen: `TEHILLIM: PRAISES.` · `150 SONGS IN FIVE BOOKS.` · `DAVID, AND OTHER VOICES.` · `WOVEN THROUGH EVERY SERVICE.` · then, large: `SONGS OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one psalm aloud. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find a short psalm. Psalm one hundred seventeen is the shortest in the whole book, just two verses. Read it out loud, slowly, even in a whisper. Then read it again. Notice how different it feels to say ancient words with your own voice. If you don't have one nearby, sit with the line we heard: at all times, praise. If you pray, you can make the psalm your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Tehillim. The Book of Psalms: one hundred and fifty songs of praise and every other feeling, linked to David and said in every Jewish prayer service.
Your line: songs of praise. Today, notice one moment that deserves a song, and give it a word of praise, out loud or inside. Day three hundred fourteen.

315.title: Planted by streams (Psalm 1)
315.hook: the one who delights in Torah is like a tree planted by streams of water
315.howItsDone: Psalm 1 is often the first psalm people learn and is read when a person or group begins reading the Psalms through; its image of the tree is a favorite in Jewish teaching about Torah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tehillim, the Book of Psalms. Your line was songs of praise. Did one moment get a word of praise? Today, we open the book at its first page. Day three hundred fifteen.

Think of a tree you know. Maybe one outside a window you've looked through for years. It's been there through heat waves and storms and whole seasons of your life. What keeps a tree like that standing? Not how tall it looks. What you can't see: the roots, and the water they've found. The Book of Psalms could have opened with thunder or kings or battles. Instead, its very first psalm opens with a person, and then a tree.
screen: `A TREE OUTSIDE YOUR WINDOW.` → `WHAT KEEPS IT STANDING?` → `THE BOOK OPENS WITH A TREE.`

segments.voice: Psalm one begins with the word ashrei: happy, or fortunate. Happy is the one who doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked, or stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of the scornful. Notice the slide: walking, then standing, then sitting. It's a picture of how people drift, first passing by, then lingering, then settling in. Instead, the psalm says, this person's delight is in the Torah of the Lord, and they meditate on it day and night. And then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither." Look at the details. Planted, not wild: someone set it there on purpose, near the water. Streams, plural: more than one source. Fruit in its season: not every day, not on demand, but when the time is right. And the leaf doesn't wither, even in dry weather. Then the contrast. The wicked are like chaff, the husks the wind blows off the threshing floor. Light, rootless, gone. The psalm isn't promising that good people never suffer. The Psalms are too honest for that. It's describing roots. A person who keeps going back to the water, day and night, grows something that holds. And it closes a week: a song without words, raising the sparks, the Maggid's circle, opponents and neighbors, the story that healed, the Psalms, and today, the tree by the stream.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit by water or a tree. If you can, go to a window with a tree in view, or sit near a plant, or run a little water in a glass and watch it. If you can't, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Look at the tree, or imagine it, and think about its roots. Now ask: where are my streams? What do I keep going back to that keeps me green? A text, a person, a practice, a place? Let one come to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
